```{r}
#| label: setup-syllabus
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(here) # project-root-relative paths
library(yaml) # read course.yml

# website/_quarto.yml is itself a project-root marker, so a bare here() would stop at
# website/ rather than the repo root. i_am() anchors it explicitly. See STYLE.md section 4.
here::i_am("website/syllabus.qmd")

cfg <- yaml::read_yaml(here("course.yml"))

# Every threshold below is DERIVED from course.yml, never typed. The 2026 spring
# syllabus stated 11 homeworks in prose and then patched itself to 10 in a callout,
# because the numbers lived in the text. They live in one file now.
n_sessions <- cfg$sessions$count
att_frac <- cfg$thresholds$attendance
att_min <- ceiling(att_frac * n_sessions)
# The lower tier of the attendance policy: the case-by-case band runs down to 60%.
att_lo_frac <- 0.60
att_lo <- ceiling(att_lo_frac * n_sessions)

n_hw <- cfg$homework$count
hw_frac <- cfg$thresholds$homework
hw_min <- ceiling(hw_frac * n_hw)

pct <- function(x) paste0(round(100 * x), "%")

shown <- function(x, fallback = "to be announced") {
  if (is.null(x) || !nzchar(x) || identical(x, "PLACEHOLDER")) fallback else x
}
exam_window <- if (identical(shown(cfg$exam$opens), "to be announced") ||
  identical(shown(cfg$exam$closes), "to be announced")) {
  "to be announced"
} else {
  paste(cfg$exam$opens, "to", cfg$exam$closes)
}
```

## Course description {#sec-course-description}

This course introduces quantitative research methods in international relations and European
integration, using modern tools for scientific programming and reproducible research.
You will learn to analyse and visualise data in R, document your work in Quarto, and manage your
projects with Git and GitHub.
Together these tools support state-of-the-art workflows for transparent, collaborative and
well-organised empirical research.
All work is done in Positron, an integrated development environment for data science.

The course teaches the Bayesian framework as its primary approach to inference.
That is a deliberate choice, not an incidental one, and it shapes how models are built,
criticised and reported throughout.

## Course objectives {#sec-course-objectives}

The overall goal is to give you the practical skills and the methodological confidence to write
an empirical bachelor thesis in political science.
You will learn to preprocess data, choose and implement appropriate models for continuous and
binary outcomes, compute quantities of interest, and interpret results accurately.

Beyond technical proficiency, the course emphasises sound statistical reasoning, effective data
visualisation, and communicating empirical findings clearly to a non-technical audience.
Through weekly assignments and a cumulative take-home exam, you will develop the ability to
evaluate statistical claims critically, in academic research and in public debate alike.

## The through-line: an 8-step Bayesian workflow {#sec-through-line}

Everything in this course builds toward one skill: running a complete Bayesian analysis end to
end.
The **take-home exam is exactly that**, on a dataset you will meet at the end.
You see the whole workflow in week 1, shown in @tbl-workflow, and deepen it each week.

{{< include slides/_workflow-8step.qmd >}}

## Course logistics {#sec-logistics}

### General information {#sec-general-information}

Each session consists of an instructor-led part on concepts and theory, followed by hands-on
exercises.
Homework is assigned at the end of class and is due `r cfg$homework$due_offset_days` days later,
before the next session.
Readings provide background, theory and context, and are linked per week from the
[Schedule](schedule.qmd).

There is **one session per week**, so there is no parallel group to switch into.
If you have to miss a session, the slides and the sample solution for that week are published on
the site, and the [Glossary](glossary.qmd) covers the terminology introduced.

### Attendance policy {#sec-attendance}

Active participation (*Mitarbeit*) is a required component of the coursework
(*Studienleistung*).
This course consists of `r n_sessions` sessions.
Successful participation is presumed if you attend at least
**`r pct(att_frac)` of sessions, that is at least `r att_min` out of `r n_sessions`**.

If attendance falls below `r pct(att_frac)` but stays at or above `r pct(att_lo_frac)`
(**`r att_lo` to `r att_min - 1` out of `r n_sessions`**), successful participation is not
presumed.
In that case the possibility of fulfilling the participation requirement is assessed case by
case.

If attendance falls below `r pct(att_lo_frac)` (**fewer than `r att_lo` out of
`r n_sessions`**), successful participation is normally considered impossible under the
examination regulations.

If sessions are cancelled during the semester, the absolute number of required sessions is
adjusted accordingly, while the percentage thresholds stay unchanged.

### Grading policy {#sec-grading}

Under the examination regulations, assessment consists of **coursework (*Studienleistung*,
pass or fail)** and a **final examination (*Prüfungsleistung*, graded)**.

Successful completion of all coursework requirements is a prerequisite for admission to the final
take-home exam.

#### Coursework (*Studienleistung*, pass or fail)

Coursework has two components, and both must be passed.

**1. Weekly homework assignments.**
There are **`r n_hw` homework assignments** over the term.
They are distributed through GitHub and assessed pass or fail.
To fulfil this requirement you must pass at least **`r pct(hw_frac)` of them, that is `r hw_min`
out of `r n_hw`**.
Homework must show a serious and complete attempt at the tasks.
A submission that is empty or clearly insufficient does not count as passed.

**2. Active participation (*Mitarbeit*).**
Active participation, as described in @sec-attendance, is a required coursework component and is
assessed pass or fail.

#### Final examination (*Prüfungsleistung*, graded)

The final examination is a **take-home exam**.

**Window:** `r exam_window`.

The exam is distributed through the `exam` repository on the course GitHub organisation, the same
template flow as the weekly homework.
You receive a dataset and a problem description for a cumulative data analysis project.

You submit a complete project repository, which must include:

- fully documented and reproducible code,
- a rendered PDF presenting your results, structured like the data, methods and analysis sections
  of a research paper,
- a statutory declaration following the
  [university's guidelines](https://www.sowi.uni-mannheim.de/media/Fakultaeten/sowi/Dokumente/Studiengangsmanagement/Eigenstaendigkeitserklaerung_Statutory_Declaration.pdf).

The state of the repository on GitHub at the moment the deadline passes is what gets evaluated.

The take-home exam is graded on the university scale, 1.0 (very good) to 5.0 (insufficient), and
it determines the overall course grade.
Every tool and workflow needed to complete it is taught during the course.

### Language and software policy {#sec-language-software}

The course is taught entirely in English and is built around R, Quarto and Git or GitHub for data
analysis, reproducible research and project management.
Work with these tools, because the exercises and workflows are designed around them.

For the take-home exam you may use another script-based language such as Python or Stata, but this
is not recommended and no guidance is provided for non-R workflows.
The emphasis is on understanding the tools, practising them, and learning to find solutions
independently.

### Hardware {#sec-hardware}

You need a computer available during class.
A standard laptop is sufficient, and there are no particular requirements for RAM, an external
GPU, or other advanced components.

If you do not own a suitable device, the University of Mannheim IT department offers a
[laptop rental service](https://www.uni-mannheim.de/en/it/students/borrowing-laptops/).
Please make use of it if you need it.

### Software {#sec-software}

Install all required software before the first session, following the separate
[installation guide](installation.qmd).
Doing it early means we can sort out any problems on day one and start the programming work
properly in the following session.

### Optional practice materials {#sec-practice-materials}

I strongly recommend making use of the DataCamp access provided with this course.
DataCamp is an online learning platform with useful opportunities to practise the material covered
here and well beyond it.
The introduction to R tutorial is a good starting point.
DataCamp courses are voluntary and are not part of the requirements to pass.

## Homework and feedback policy {#sec-feedback-policy}

> **A sample solution is published for every homework. Individual feedback is NOT provided by
> default.** The only individual feedback available is the **optional AI feedback** you can opt
> into by adding an open-source `license.md` to your submission repo.

**What that means in practice.**
A sample solution is published for every homework after its due date, and it is the standard
against which you should read your own work.
Individual comments on individual submissions are not part of this course by default.

**Opting in to AI feedback.**
If you add an open-source `license.md` to your submission repository, you opt in to automated,
individualised feedback.
An AI reads your submission alongside the sample solution and writes a `FEEDBACK.qmd` and
`FEEDBACK.pdf` back into your repository, organised by the eight workflow steps.
No `license.md` means no processing at all.
This is entirely optional, and opting out costs you nothing beyond the individual feedback
itself.

### Late work policy {#sec-late-work}

Late submissions are not accepted.
If you anticipate any difficulty in meeting a deadline, discuss it with me **before** the
deadline, not after.

### AI policy {#sec-ai-policy}

All submissions are checked for plagiarism, and violations of the code of conduct may result in
failing the course or in expulsion.

Generative AI tools such as ChatGPT or Gemini are permitted for the final examination, but any
AI-generated content or code must be clearly marked, thoroughly commented, and accompanied by the
chat history, so that your understanding is demonstrable.
I will give occasional guidance on using AI responsibly.
Relying on it from the start does hinder learning:
[research suggests AI helps most those who already understand the topic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.03102).
For a fuller explanation of why AI can undermine learning, see
[this piece by Andrew Heiss](https://governancef25.classes.andrewheiss.com/syllabus.html#ai-large-language-models-and-bullshit).

::: {.callout-note}
**Two different things, both involving AI.**
The policy above is about AI *you* use while doing your own work, which must be disclosed and
commented.
The opt-in feedback described in @sec-feedback-policy is different: it is run by me, on an
explicit `license.md` opt-in, and it comments on work you have already submitted.
Using the feedback pipeline is never something you need to declare.
:::

### Mental health support {#sec-mental-health}

Life and study at the University of Mannheim can sometimes feel complicated, challenging, or
overwhelming.
That is completely normal.
You are not expected to understand or memorise course content on the first attempt.

If you ever feel mentally or emotionally strained, you may find useful advice on the university's
[good mental health and studying page](https://www.uni-mannheim.de/en/academics/studying-the-healthy-way/good-mental-health/).
The [help in times of crisis page](https://www.uni-mannheim.de/en/academics/studying-the-healthy-way/help-in-times-of-crisis/)
gives an overview of the counselling and support services available at the university.
